rockchip/rk3399: Fix rkclk_init() to actually use PERILP1_PCLK_HZ This patch fixes a typo in the clock initialization code that caused the PERILP1_PCLK_HZ constant to be ignored and the clock to always run at the same speed as its parent (PERILP1_HCLK_HZ). cros_build_lib.py: tolerate tar modification check failure The tar program exits with code 1 if (and only if) it detects that the modification time of the file or directory it is archiving changes between the beginning and the end of reading it. Thus if, for instance, a temporary file is created and removed, the check will fail for that directory. This can catch valid races but can also produce spurious errors. We are too chicken to ignore these errors (perhaps rightfully so), so we try again but only once. (Note that check isn't offering reliable protection. The modification can happen after tar has processed the file or directory, in which case it goes unnoticed. A separate strategy is needed to isolate and fix this problem.) power: memory_suspend_test: Use 2.7 GB as fallback, not 2.9 GB It appears that 2.9 GB isn't quite guaranteed to pass in 32-bit userspace on all systems. Let's be a little more conservative and go down to 2.7 GB. If there are really memory errors this will be almost as likely to catch them anyway and then we don't have to try to fiddle more. Note: from testing in python, the max I could allocate on rk3399-kevin was about 0xab175000 bytes. Specifically: >>> import ctypes >>> libc = ctypes.CDLL("libc.so.6") >>> p = libc.malloc(0xab175000); p; libc.free(p) 32776 0 >>> p = libc.malloc(0xab176000); p; libc.free(p) 0 0 From above, max: 2,870,431,744 bytes. 2800 * 1024 * 1024: 2,936,012,800 bytes. 2700 * 1024 * 1024: 2,831,155,200 bytes. NOTE: it's possible (probable) that we can actually go higher than 0xab175000 bytes in C code (because of the missing python overhead), but let's just be safe and stick with something that should definitely work. BUG=chromium:638755 TEST=suspend_stress_test --memory_check no longer crashes. CHROMIUM: drm/rockchip: Do not modify plane state in .atomic_update The .atomic_update callback is responsible from updating hardware configuration based on the state and is not supposed to alter the state. Current code calculates part of the state late in .atomic_update, which not only violates the above principle, but also causes a race with frame start interrupt, which compares yrgb_mst of current state and active value in hardware register to determine if flush has taken place. This patch fixes the problem by moving yrgb_mst calculation to .atomic_check callback, which is where some low level state preparation should be happening.
